Surface engineering strategies
Surface engineering is a central strategy for overcom­
ing the intrinsic limitations of g-C₃N₄ and adapting its 
physicochemical properties to the complex require­
ments of cancer therapy. Recent studies have explored 
a range of modification approaches, including hetero­
atom doping, heterojunction construction, noble-metal 
decoration, oxygen-vacancy engineering, and surface 
functionalization [75]. These strategies can regulate the 
electronic structure, band-edge positions, charge-carrier 
separation, light absorption, surface reactivity, colloidal 
stability, and biological interactions of g-C₃N₄, thereby 
influencing its photocatalytic and therapeutic behav­
ior (Fig. 2). Importantly, surface engineering does not 
simply aim to maximize photocatalytic activity. Ratio­
nal modification should establish a balance among light 
utilization, charge separation, ROS generation, catalytic 
stability, tumor accumulation, cellular uptake, and bio­

Recent studies have emphasized that the photocatalytic 
behavior of g-C₃N₄ is determined not only by its nomi­
nal bandgap but also by the positions of the band edges, 
defect states, charge-carrier dynamics, and surface elec­
tronic structure [23]. Bandgap and electronic-structure 
engineering represent an important strategy for over­
coming these intrinsic limitations. Approaches includ­
ing heteroatom doping, vacancy engineering, structural 
disorder, functional-group modification and incorpora­
tion of metallic or semiconductor components can alter 
the electronic structure, band positions, charge density 
and carrier-transfer pathways of g-C₃N₄ [24]. In particu­
lar, defect engineering can introduce localized electronic 
states and modulate charge-carrier dynamics, thereby 
offering opportunities to enhance light harvesting and 
facilitate photogenerated charge transfer. However, the 
influence of defects is highly dependent on their type,

However, future designs should move beyond maxi­
mizing photocatalytic activity alone and instead establish 
quantitative relationships between material properties, 
ROS identity and localization, therapeutic mechanisms,

or other light-conversion components may extend the 
optical response of g-C₃N₄ toward longer wavelengths.

Photocatalytic mechanisms for cancer therapy
Reactive oxygen species generation
The photocatalytic activity of g-C₃N₄-based nanomateri­
als is primarily associated with their ability to generate 
reactive oxygen species (ROS) under appropriate light 
irradiation [59]. Upon absorption of photons with ener­
gies exceeding the effective bandgap, electrons are pro­
moted from the valence band (VB) to the conduction 
band (CB), leaving photogenerated holes in the VB. The 
subsequent generation, migration, separation, and inter­
facial transfer of these charge carriers determine both the 
quantity and chemical identity of the ROS produced at 
the nanomaterial–biological interface [60].
Importantly, the therapeutic consequences of ROS gen­
eration depend not only on the total ROS level but also 
on ROS identity, lifetime, diffusion range, and subcellular 
site of formation.
Photogenerated electrons in the CB can reduce dis­
